title: FBI 1992: Lanning's 'Investigator's Guide to Ritual Child Abuse'
summary: Supervisory Special Agent Kenneth V. Lanning (Behavioral Science Unit): no evidence of large-scale organized satanic cults abusing children in the US; crimes with bizarre/ritualistic elements do occur and must be distinguished from organized-cult claims; warned against suggestive interviewing. Frequently misquoted as a 'seven-year FBI study' — it is an investigator's guide, and Lanning did not declare all such claims a hoax.
tldr: This source is only page 20 of Lanning's 1992 'Investigator's Guide' — it shows Lanning pushing back on over-broad 'ritual abuse' labels (preferring 'bizarre' to 'ritual,' and 'multidimensional child sex rings'), noting alleged experts on such cases had never actually handled one before ('the answer was always the same — none!').
ai_summary:
AI review of the Wikisource transcription of page 20 of Kenneth V. Lanning's 1992 'Investigator's Guide to Allegations of "Ritual" Child Abuse' (FBI Behavioral Science Unit), read in full:
- Victims' reports covered 'ceremonies, chanting, robes and costumes, drugs, use of urine and feces, animal sacrifice, torture, abduction, mutilation, murder, and even cannibalism and vampirism'; Lanning argues 'bizarre is probably preferable to the word ritual to describe this activity' since ritual implies occult/satanic motivation.
- He notes 'experts' who 'will stake his or her professional reputation on the fact that the victims are telling the truth' — but when asked how many such cases they had evaluated before, 'the answer was always the same — none!' These experts had only handled one-on-one intrafamilial cases.
- He coins 'multidimensional child sex rings' for these cases, noting 40–50% of reported offenders are women (vs. almost all men in historical rings), many are 'situational molesters' rather than preferential pedophiles, and victims are both boys and girls.
- Caveat: this is a single page, not the full report — the record summary's broader claims (the guide's full conclusions; that it's 'frequently misquoted as a seven-year FBI study') are consistent in spirit but not established on this page alone.
